documents: Rebay, Powell & Holland (2022), Calculated phase equilibria for high-pressure serpentinites and compositionally related rocks close to the MASH system, J. Metamorph. Geol. 40, 1219–1234 (published PDF)

entry.evidence: calculated using the Holland and Powell data set, tc-ds62, and new activity–composition relations for antigorite and talc

sequences.source_document: Rebay, Powell & Holland (2022), J. Metamorph. Geol. 40, 1219–1234 (published PDF)

steps.action: Summarized the experimentally and petrologically established stability ranges of serpentine polymorphs, brucite and antigorite-bearing assemblages from published work.
steps.quote: Such a general view of the stability of serpentinite mineral assemblages was built up through experimental studies in simple systems

steps.action: Posed the need for a backbone-system context (PT projections and compatibility diagrams) for pseudosection modelling of serpentinites and whiteschists, with MASH as that backbone.
steps.quote: However, a way to provide context for pseudosections is via calculated PT projections and compatibility diagrams.

steps.action: Built new activity–composition models for antigorite and talc following Powell et al. (2014) and combined them with THERMOCALC tc340, data set tc-ds62 and the White et al. (2014) models.
steps.quote: augmented by new models for antigorite and talc constructed using the approach of Powell et al. (2014)

steps.action: Recalibrated antigorite, phase A and clinohumite properties: used new compressibilities, rejected inconsistent experiments, and raised Bromiley and Pawley's temperatures for thermocouple pressure effects, reversing their earlier omission (Appendix A.1).
steps.quote: The combination of adjusted temperature in the Bromiley and Pawley (2003) runs and the new compressibilities of antigorite led to a much improved calibration

steps.action: Checked the premise that Al has only a marginal effect on antigorite stability using the consistency of fits to three independent low-Al experimental data sets (Appendix A.1).
steps.quote: the close consistency of the fits to the experiments of Bromiley and Pawley (2003), Komabayashi et al. (2005) and Wunder and Schreyer (1997)

steps.action: Kept the White et al. (2014) chlorite model despite its poor fit for subaluminous chlorite, replacing only the f3clin DQF with 40 kJ because the published value gave inappropriate ferric contents (Appendix A.2).
steps.quote: gives completely inappropriate ferric contents for chlorite. Instead, a value of 40 kJ is adopted.

steps.action: Set talc interaction energies by analogy and solvus constraints, and varied W(tats,tap) in the data set fit to measured experimental talc compositions (Appendix A.3).
steps.quote: was varied in the data set fitting

steps.action: Calculated the MSH PT projection with compatibility diagrams (Figure 1), then the MASH projection (Figure 2) with antigorite, talc and talc+kyanite reactions highlighted (Figure 3).
steps.quote: Adding Al2O3 to the MSH system, a MASH PT projection, shown in Figure 2, allows all relevant phases in the rocks to be considered

steps.action: Compared the calculated persistence of chlorite after antigorite breakdown with natural chlorite-harzburgites and experiments reported in the literature.
steps.quote: as observed in many examples of metamorphic chlorite-harzburgites from HP terrains and in experiments

steps.action: Calculated MASH + H2O compatibility diagrams at 25 kbar for 520, 600, 680 and 760 °C (Figure 4) to trace assemblage changes with temperature.
steps.quote: Compatibility diagrams for the MASH system with H2O in excess, in Figure 4

steps.action: Compared the calculated chlorite–olivine–orthopyroxene assemblage after antigorite-out with the occurrence of chlorite-harzburgites in HP–UHP terrains.
steps.quote: such metamorphic chlorite-harzburgites are widespread in HP to UHP terrains

steps.action: Calculated T–X sections projected from chlorite (Figure 5), then added FeO to obtain the FMASH PT projection (Figure 6) and a compatibility diagram at 25 kbar and 600 °C (Figure 7).
steps.quote: On addition of FeO, MASH invariant points become FMASH univariant reactions

steps.action: Qualified how FMASH results apply to serpentinites: storing Fe as magnetite shifts effective compositions towards Mg-rich values.
steps.quote: This is reflected in an effective shift of the composition of the rocks towards more Mg-rich compositions in FMASH once magnetite is discounted.

steps.action: Added CaO to calculate the CMASH projection (Figures S1, S2) and compared antigorite and talc+kyanite reactions across MASH, FMASH and CMASH (Figures 8, 9).
steps.quote: it is necessary to add CaO as a component to MASH

steps.action: Took the bulk composition of an HP serpentinite from the first author's earlier Western Alps study as input for a CFMASHO pseudosection.
steps.quote: calculated for an HP serpentinite from Rebay et al. (2012)

steps.action: Calculated a PT pseudosection for the serpentinite composition with H2O in excess (Figure 10).
steps.quote: The pseudosection reflects fully the MASH–CMASH grids

steps.action: Compared the pseudosection with natural occurrences: rare brucite in orogenic serpentinites, di–atg–ol–chl in Western Alps cold-subduction rocks, and chlorite-harzburgite in the Alps, Almirez and China.
steps.quote: This is consistent with brucite being found very rarely in metamorphic serpentinites in orogens.

steps.action: Took the composition of whiteschist sample DM1035 from Ferrando et al. (2009), excluding K, as input for a second pseudosection.
steps.quote: calculated for a whiteschist, sample DM1035 from Ferrando et al. (2009), excluding K

steps.action: Calculated a CFMASHO pseudosection for the whiteschist (Figure 11), including the CASH lawsonite-breakdown univariant line.
steps.quote: An interesting feature of this diagram is the presence of a univariant line

steps.action: Compared the calculated garnet–kyanite–talc field with the principal assemblage observed in the sample.
steps.quote: which corresponds to the principal mineral assemblage observed in the rock, is quite large

steps.action: Described a calculated divariant boundary [-ctd] that crosses the lawsonite = zoisite + kyanite + quartz univariant, apparently against usual topology rules (Figure S4).
steps.quote: This peculiar feature will not have visible consequences in rocks but is here described for the first time.

steps.action: Kept MASH as the backbone of serpentinite and whiteschist phase relations, with Fe shifting conditions and Ca needed for clinopyroxene, amphibole and garnet.
steps.quote: The backbone system MASH shows the main reactions in these rock compositions.

tree.answer: Stability of mineral assemblages in HP serpentinites and whiteschists, known from experiments and rocks
No; equilibria are calculated from thermodynamic data and a–x models
Provide backbone context (PT projections, compatibility diagrams) for pseudosection modelling
Conditions set computationally (P, T, chemical system, bulk composition)
Only qualitative agreement with cited natural assemblages and experiments; no sensitivity tests on model parameters
Diagrams kept as backbone context for serpentinite and whiteschist modelling

end.claim: Phase relations calculated with tc-ds62 and new antigorite and talc a–x models give MASH as a backbone for HP serpentinite and whiteschist equilibria: brucite is consumed from about 450 °C and antigorite up to about 680 °C, Fe shifts conditions without changing topology, and Ca is required for clinopyroxene, amphibole and garnet.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the new antigorite and talc activity–composition models, and the recalibrated antigorite data in tc-ds62, none of the calculated projections, compatibility diagrams or pseudosections could be drawn.

gates.evidence: No data were acquired. The calculations follow from the aim of mapping backbone phase relations, not from a stated hypothesis. The main claim meets only qualitative consistency checks against cited natural assemblages and experiments (pp. 1222, 1223, 1227, 1228), which could have failed but were not set up as tests. Nothing was fixed in advance; talc and antigorite parameters were tuned in data-set fitting (pp. 1232–1233).

imports.item: Symmetric (regular-solution) formalism for interaction energies in mineral solid-solution models (Powell & Holland 1993)
Phase-rule (Schreinemakers) topology rules for univariant and divariant equilibria

novelty_claims.quote: This peculiar feature will not have visible consequences in rocks but is here described for the first time.

limits:
1. Model uncertainty and sensitivity. The authors state that the thermodynamic descriptions, especially antigorite, are rather uncertain (p. 1231). Calculated subaluminous chlorite y values are too high by up to 0.1, an unresolved problem (p. 1233). No sensitivity test shows how these uncertainties move the reported reaction temperatures (inference: the stated temperatures carry unquantified uncertainty).
2. Comparisons with nature. All are qualitative, against observations cited from other studies or from the authors' earlier work. No quantitative misfit is reported.
3. Fitting not shown. The recalibration of antigorite in tc-ds62 and the talc fit are described, but fit statistics and residuals are not given.
4. Missing documents. The supplement (Figures S1–S4, reaction tables, pre-existing models) was not supplied. No review file was supplied, though two reviewers and an editor are acknowledged, so no review sequence is coded.
5. Sub-claims and their statuses. The dehydration temperature ranges (brucite out from about 450 °C, antigorite out up to about 680 °C) are calculated ranges without uncertainty (closest to estimate_with_resolution, but no resolution is given). The novel [-ctd] topology feature is a calculated feature, not checked in rocks.
6. Composition is none_fits. The walk is a forward computational mapping of phase space enabled by a new capability. There is no rival, no crucial test and no observation-led establishment of a phenomenon, so capability_first does not strictly apply.
7. Ordering. Appendix-only calibration steps (4–7) are placed after the capability step they support.

disagreements.target: Most recent studies using older thermodynamic data sets and simplistic a–x relations (e.g., Padrón-Navarta et al., 2013)
disagreements.support: The authors offer a recent internally consistent data set and a consistent set of a–x relations built with the Powell et al. (2014) approach.
disagreements.quote: most recent studies use older thermodynamic data sets and simplistic a–x relations

disagreements.target: Antigorite stability experiments of Bose and Navrotsky (1998) and Ulmer and Trommsdorff (1995)
disagreements.support: Reassessment using the Nestola et al. (2009) compressibilities found these experiments inconsistent with the overall data-set fit.
disagreements.quote: has led to the rejection of the experiments of Bose and Navrotsky (1998) and Ulmer and Trommsdorff (1995)

disagreements.target: Reported run temperatures of Bromiley and Pawley (2003)
disagreements.support: Following Komabayashi et al. (2005) and Takahashi et al. (1993), the Pt–Rh thermocouple pressure effect requires raising temperatures by up to 25 °C at 50 kbar.
disagreements.quote: the temperature of Bromiley and Pawley’s experiments require raising

disagreements.support: With the temperature correction the experiments are now included, giving a much improved antigorite calibration.
disagreements.quote: had earlier been omitted from the analysis of Holland and Powell (2011) because their temperatures appeared too low at high pressure

disagreements.target: Debate on the effect of Al on antigorite stability
disagreements.support: Close fits to three experimental data sets using low-Al antigorite indicate the effect is marginal for small Al contents.
disagreements.quote: for small Al contents, the effect is probably only marginal.
